title: KV cache architecture eviction and paging deep dive with Nova Insights
summary: Deep dive on Redwood's KV cache behavior for long-context workloads; investigated eviction triggers observed by Nova Insights, discussed paging vs eviction tradeoffs, prefix reuse effects, batching/latency implications, and on-prem/VPC considerations. Agreed to run targeted benchmark with synthetic long-context traces and follow up with detailed eviction logs and proposed config changes.
next_steps: Redwood: share KV eviction diagnostic script and sample logs by 2027-05-13
Nova: run synthetic long-context trace and share results by 2027-05-17
Schedule follow-up benchmark session week of 2027-05-24 (Priya/Alex + Maya/Sam)
Exchange security docs for private deployment (Redwood to send SSO/SOC2 packet)
action_items: Priya Shah: prepare eviction diagnostic script + sample runbook (due 2027-05-13)
Maya Chen: provide 3 representative long-context traces and current token distribution (due 2027-05-17)
Alex Kim: send pricing/POC options and cadence for Dedicated capacity (due 2027-05-14)
Sam Patel: collect p99 latency targets and current SLA constraints (due 2027-05-15)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-10
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Nova CTO), Sam Patel (Nova SRE), Maya Chen (Nova ML Engineer), Riley Grant (Product)

[00:00:05] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we scheduled about 50 minutes, deep dive on the kv-cache behavior you've been seeing, especially the eviction and paging during the long conversations. does that still match everybody's expectations?

[00:00:15] Jordan Lee: yeah that's perfect. we ran into this on prod last week - early tokens are cached, but once sessions hit ~12k tokens we see a big jump in p95 latency and some token gaps in responses.

[00:00:28] Priya Shah: ok got it. can you describe what you mean by "token gaps" - are responses truncating or re-fetching from origin?

[00:00:33] Sam Patel: it's kind of both - sometimes the model stalls for a second and then continues, other times we see repeated re-generation on the same prefix which suggests the kv cache evicted and then got paged back slowly.

[00:00:45] Diego Ramos: (interrupting) just to set expectations: when the kv cache evicts, you'll either hit an on-disk paging path or re-compute depending on the config. paging will have higher latency but avoid recompute; eviction + recompute will be even worse for long sequences.

[00:00:58] Maya Chen: hi, quick note: our workload is chat-like but with long context - user docs + full convo history, avg session length 9k tokens, tails at 25k for high-value accounts.

[00:01:10] Alex Kim: thanks. so we'll walk through architecture, observed behavior, a few hypotheses, and then a recommended benchmark plan. maybe Priya can start with the architecture diagram?

[00:01:22] Priya Shah: sure. so our KV cache is segmented by request key (we call it session id) and by layer/attention head slice; we maintain a hot in-RAM LRU with policy based on total KV size and per-GPU mem budget. beyond the in-memory limit we have a spill-to-disk paging layer (optionally on local NVMe or network store) and an eviction policy that prunes oldest or least-recently-used depending on config.

[00:01:48] Jordan Lee: so you have both paging and eviction? i thought it was one or the other.

[00:01:52] Priya Shah: it's both - paging is a softer degradation where we keep keys but move them to slower storage; eviction is permanent removal of keys and will cause recomputation of kv when needed.

[00:02:05] Riley Grant: are there heuristics to prefer paging over eviction? we've seen behaviors that look like eviction even though we have nvme enabled.

[00:02:12] Priya Shah: good question. heuristics include current memory pressure across the GPU pool, expected re-use frequency (we estimate reuse via prefix reuse counters), and a config knob for "prefer paging" if you want to accept p99 spikes rather than recompute. it also depends on fragmentation and whether keys are contiguous; small scattered keys sometimes get evicted to reduce metadata overhead.

[00:02:34] Sam Patel: this matches our suspicion - when multiple sessions share prefixes (we do a lot of prompt templating) the reuse should be high but we still get evictions. could fragmentation cause eviction of big prefixes?

[00:02:44] Priya Shah: yes fragmentation can. if the cache allocator can't allocate a contiguous block for a new kv slice, it might evict older slices to defragment. we do compaction periodically but it's a tradeoff with CPU overhead.

[00:02:56] Maya Chen: are there config knobs we can tune right now? like change eviction to lru vs size-based or bump the in-memory threshold?

[00:03:03] Alex Kim: yes, and we'll list those in the runbook. typical levers: increase in-memory cache limit (if you have spare GPU RAM), enable prefer-paging, increase compaction frequency (costs CPU), and tune per-session lifetime.

[00:03:17] Priya Shah: also model-side things: quantization profile affects KV size - 8-bit vs 4-bit changes memory footprint and eviction behavior. if you're on a quantized model that stores larger KV entries, that can push you into eviction faster.

[00:03:30] Jordan Lee: we are running a 4-bit quantized variant. do you recommend moving to 8-bit for KV storage? that seems counterintuitive.

[00:03:36] Priya Shah: sorry, typo - 4-bit reduces model weight memory but sometimes the runtime stores KV in a higher-precision format for compute stability, depending on kernel. for some models the KV ends up being 16-bit which increases footprint. we can confirm exact format in your deployment.

[00:03:49] Sam Patel: (crosstalk) yeah we saw notes in the onboarding doc about "kv format variability" - would like that clarified.

[00:03:55] Alex Kim: action item - we'll share a table of KV storage formats per model and kernel by 2027-05-13.

[00:04:03] [00:04:05] Diego Ramos: shifting gears: prefix reuse - we instrument a reuse score per prefix. high reuse prefixes are promoted to a hot lane; they get pinning for a configurable window. if your templated prompts cause identical prefixes across sessions, they should get pinned and avoid eviction.

[00:04:25] Maya Chen: but in practice identical prefixes sometimes don't match because of small metadata differences (timestamps, session ids). can Redwood's prefix normalization help?

[00:04:32] Priya Shah: yes, we have lightweight normalization rules you can enable that strip volatile tokens from the prefix key. that increases effective reuse but needs careful rule design to avoid merging unrelated contexts.

[00:04:44] Jordan Lee: ok that's promising. what about the paging latency - when we hit NVMe paging we saw a 700ms spike - is that expected?

[00:04:52] Diego Ramos: NVMe can be sub-100ms in our best-case but when multiple pages are requested concurrently or the NVMe queue is saturated, latency climbs. also network NVMe (e.g., remote store) adds unpredictability. 700ms isn't outlandish under load, but it's an area we can optimize with prefetch heuristics and batching.

[00:05:09] Sam Patel: prefetch? how does that work for unpredictable user behavior?

[00:05:12] Priya Shah: we use a predictive prefetcher that samples session access patterns - if a session typically references older tokens at certain steps, we preemptively page them in. it reduces worst-case spikes but increases background IO. you can tune aggressiveness.

[00:05:30] [00:05:35] Alex Kim: i'd like to jump to the logs you shared. Maya, you sent an eviction trace and a p99 spike capture?

[00:05:40] Maya Chen: yes - link in the calendar invite, file named nv_eviction_trace_may3.log. the pattern shows a set of sessions all sharing a common prefix template and then a burst of user uploads that change token distributions. the eviction windows align with a GC job in our cluster but timing isn't exact.

[00:06:00] Priya Shah: looking at the sample, i see repeated evictions of the same prefix across machines - that suggests inconsistent prefix hashing across the pool or session routing flipping between GPUs, causing loss of locality. are you using sticky routing?

[00:06:12] Sam Patel: we're using round-robin to balance load - we didn't realize locality mattered for KV reuse.

[00:06:17] Alex Kim: that's a big one - if session requests go to different GPUs you lose in-memory KV locality and will frequently page or recompute. we recommend sticky routing per session id for stateful workloads.

[00:06:29] Jordan Lee: what are the tradeoffs for sticky routing? we worry about hot-shards and uneven load.

[00:06:34] Diego Ramos: tradeoff is load skew; mitigate with consistent hashing, session affinity windows, and spillover policies. you can set a max sessions-per-GPU threshold and overflow to other GPUs when overloaded. also combine with cross-GPU KV sharing options like deduplicated remote cache for cold prefixes.

[00:06:52] [00:07:00] Maya Chen: on the topic of recompute vs paging - recompute means re-running key generation for earlier tokens which increases CPU/GPU cycles. we saw cost blowups when eviction happened for popular sessions. any recommendations to limit cost?

[00:07:12] Priya Shah: yes, cost levers: prefer paging over eviction, increase pin window for hot prefixes, enable deduplication across sessions (store single copy of identical prefix KV), and tune batch sizes to amortize KV recompute cost. also consider Dedicated reserved capacity if you have predictable high-usage accounts.

[00:07:30] Alex Kim: quick FYI: Dedicated pools allow you to set higher in-memory KV budgets per GPU and avoid noisy neighbor eviction; we can include Dedicated cost estimates in the follow-up.

[00:07:39] Riley Grant: that would help. also curious about private deployment - if we run on-prem, does Redwood still handle the runtime patches and updated kernels?

[00:07:46] Priya Shah: yes for Private we provide an update channel for the control plane and runtime artifacts; for strict air-gapped setups we provide signed tarballs and upgrade scripts. KV behavior is identical but you control hardware choices (NVMe config, network fabric) which influence paging performance.

[00:08:00] Sam Patel: good to know. any recommended NVMe specs? we currently use shared iSCSI-backed disks.

[00:08:05] Diego Ramos: local NVMe on each host is best for lowest paging latency. spec: enterprise NVMe with sustained IOPS and >1GB/s read bandwidth per device; also ensure IO queue depths and CPU affinity are tuned. Network-backed stores need fast network adapters and low-latency fabric.

[00:08:22] Jordan Lee: noted.

[00:08:25] [00:09:00] (brief screen share of a dashboard)

[00:09:05] Priya Shah: i'm showing an instrumentation view - prefix reuse heatmap, eviction counters per GPU, and paging histogram. in your trace i can see a cluster of prefixes with high reuse that still got evicted because they fell below the pin threshold when a background burst of large ephemeral sessions arrived.

[00:09:27] Maya Chen: so if we increase the pin threshold slightly, those high-value prefixes would remain in-memory?

[00:09:31] Priya Shah: yes, but you pay memory. it's a capacity planning question: which prefixes are business-critical? we can help you annotate prefixes coming from paid accounts to prioritize them.

[00:09:43] Sam Patel: annotation - can that be automated? we have account metadata in our routing layer.

[00:09:48] Diego Ramos: yes, you can attach tags to session keys and our cache accepts policy overrides: e.g., tag "paid" -> auto-pin for 24 hours. that's a common enterprise pattern.

[00:09:58] Jordan Lee: excellent.

[00:10:05] [00:10:30] Alex Kim: let's validate our hypotheses: (1) routing is causing lost locality; (2) fragmentation and compaction behavior causing evictions; (3) KV storage format is larger than expected due to runtime conversions; (4) paging queue saturation spikes latency. we propose a benchmark plan - Priya, can you outline the test?

[00:10:47] Priya Shah: test plan summary: two-phase test. phase A: routing/locality validation - replay sampled production sessions with sticky routing vs round-robin and collect eviction/paging counters. phase B: long-context stress - synthetic traces up to 30k tokens with NVMe enabled vs disabled and quantization format variations. measure p50/p95/p99 latency, paging IO, and compute delta in GPU cycles. we'll provide scripts and a runbook.

[00:11:12] Maya Chen: how long does phase B take? we have to schedule hardware windows.

[00:11:16] Priya Shah: per-run ~2 hours for full envelope; we'll give a lightweight 30-minute smoke first. total recommended is ~8 hours for thorough coverage.

[00:11:25] Alex Kim: we'll also include a small canary change: enable prefix normalization in a test cluster to measure reuse uplift.

[00:11:32] Sam Patel: sounds good. what metrics should we share back? eviction counts, paging latency histogram, prefix reuse rate, and per-session p99 tail.

[00:11:39] Priya Shah: yes, include token distribution and a sample of sessions that hit >20k tokens.

[00:11:45] [00:12:10] Riley Grant: one more question - we have concerns around audit/logging for evictions for compliance. does Redwood capture eviction events with enough metadata?

[00:12:18] Diego Ramos: we log eviction events with session key (hashed), reason code (LRU/fragmentation/force), GPU id, and timestamp. for Private deployments we can increase retention and include raw traces in your S3. for hosted, we mask session identifiers but can provide hashed references for debugging.

[00:12:34] Jordan Lee: hashed references are ok but we may need PII-free trace mapping. we'll follow up with a security request.

[00:12:40] Alex Kim: action item - send security docs + eviction logging spec.

[00:12:45] [00:13:00] (long pause, people check notes)

[00:13:05] Maya Chen: quick nit - we see some misalignment between model sequence length and the runtime's reported seq-len; could that cause partial kv writes?

[00:13:12] Priya Shah: partial writes should not happen but occasionally a mismatch in tokenizer pre-processing vs runtime tokenization yields observed differences. we added a small checksum in newer runtimes to detect and reject mismatched KV writes; please confirm your tokenization pipeline version.

[00:13:28] Sam Patel: we use the in-house tokenizer that tweaks whitespace normalization. we'll run a parity test.

[00:13:33] Alex Kim: ok, next: cost implications. Jordan, do you have cost constraints we should be aware of for proposed Dedicated or increased memory budgets?

[00:13:40] Jordan Lee: budget is flexible for high-value users but we need a clear ROI. if the Dedicated option reduces p99 to <150ms and cuts recompute costs by half for our top 5% sessions, it's likely justifiable.

[00:13:52] Diego Ramos: we can model that. Alex will send a cost vs perf spreadsheet.

[00:13:58] Alex Kim: noted.

[00:14:05] [00:14:20] (they share a small checklist in chat)

[00:14:25] Priya Shah: any other deep technical questions?

[00:14:30] Riley Grant: what about the KV eviction threshold being dynamic - can we set policies by account tier?

[00:14:35] Priya Shah: yes, policy overrides by tag as discussed. you can map account tier to pin windows and prefer-paging flags. we'll include examples in the runbook.

[00:14:44] Maya Chen: one more: for long-context streaming where we do partial decode as tokens arrive, does Redwood preserve KV across partial windows or is there recompute at window boundaries?

[00:14:53] Diego Ramos: we support continuous KV append - we keep the full KV for the session and append new keys. windowing can be configured for memory reduction, but by default we preserve KV across streaming windows.

[00:15:05] Sam Patel: ok that clarifies the streaming behavior.

[00:15:10] [00:15:30] Alex Kim: i'm going to recap quickly and confirm owners: (1) Priya share diagnostic script and runbook by 5/13; (2) Alex send cost model and Dedicated estimates by 5/14; (3) Nova provide long-context traces and token distribution by 5/17; (4) schedule bench for week of 5/24. does that capture it?

[00:15:37] Jordan Lee: yes, that works.

[00:15:42] Maya Chen: a couple of quick clarifying questions on the runbook outputs - can the scripts output per-token reuse histograms?

[00:15:48] Priya Shah: yes - per-token reuse + prefix-level reuse histograms are included.

[00:15:52] Riley Grant: and sample config patches we can apply to test clusters?

[00:15:55] Priya Shah: yes.

[00:16:00] (end of formal portion; small social chat)

[00:16:06] Diego Ramos: thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the artifacts.

[00:16:10] Jordan Lee: appreciate it. good session.

[00:16:15] Alex Kim: cool. closing notes: shared artifacts - nv_eviction_trace_may3.log (customer), redwood_kv_runbook_v1.pdf (redwood), benchmark_scripts.tar.gz (redwood internal link).

[00:16:28] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "KV" transcribed as "K V" in a few places; speaker attribution defaulted to names provided in the calendar but may not match exact speaker ordering.
